checks.title: Password maximum age is 365 days or less
checks.rationale: Forcing periodic password changes limits the window an already-compromised password stays useful, though CIS notes this is less important when MFA is in use.
checks.remediation: Set 'PASS_MAX_DAYS 365' in /etc/login.defs (existing accounts also need: chage --maxdays 365 <user>)

checks.title: Password minimum age is at least 1 day
checks.rationale: Without a minimum age, a user can immediately change a new password back to their old one, defeating password-history rotation policies.
checks.remediation: Set 'PASS_MIN_DAYS 1' in /etc/login.defs (existing accounts also need: chage --mindays 1 <user>)

checks.title: Password expiration warning is at least 7 days
checks.rationale: Warning users before their password expires avoids surprise lockouts, which otherwise tend to get 'fixed' by disabling expiry entirely - a worse outcome.
checks.remediation: Set 'PASS_WARN_AGE 7' in /etc/login.defs (existing accounts also need: chage --warndays 7 <user>)

checks.title: No accounts have an empty password field in /etc/shadow
checks.rationale: An empty password field (2nd colon-delimited field in /etc/shadow) means PAM may allow that account to log in with no password at all, depending on nullok settings.
checks.evidence: /etc/shadow could not be read (requires root) - cannot verify password fields.
checks.remediation: passwd -l <user>  # lock any account found with an empty password field, or set a real password with passwd <user>

checks.title: No duplicate UID 0 (root-equivalent) accounts exist besides root
checks.rationale: Any account sharing UID 0 has full root privileges regardless of its username - this is a classic backdoor technique and should never occur outside of 'root' itself.
checks.remediation: Investigate any extra UID-0 account immediately; usually: usermod -u <new-unique-uid> <account>  or delete it with userdel if unauthorized.

checks.title: Root account's default group is GID 0
checks.rationale: root's primary group should be the root group (GID 0), matching standard system convention; a different primary group is unusual and worth investigating (could indicate tampering or a broken account migration).
checks.remediation: usermod -g 0 root

checks.title: /etc/passwd permissions are 644 or more restrictive, owned by root:root
checks.rationale: /etc/passwd is world-readable by design (it holds no secrets since shadow passwords split hashes into /etc/shadow), but must not be writable by non-root users or accounts could be tampered with.
checks.remediation: chown root:root /etc/passwd && chmod 644 /etc/passwd

checks.title: /etc/shadow permissions are 640 or more restrictive, owned by root:shadow
checks.rationale: /etc/shadow holds password hashes. If it is readable by non-root users, an attacker can take the hashes offline and crack them.
checks.remediation: chown root:shadow /etc/shadow && chmod 640 /etc/shadow

checks.title: /etc/group permissions are 644 or more restrictive, owned by root:root
checks.rationale: /etc/group defines group membership; if it's writable by non-root users, a user could add themselves to a privileged group.
checks.remediation: chown root:root /etc/group && chmod 644 /etc/group

checks.title: /etc/gshadow permissions are 640 or more restrictive, owned by root:shadow
checks.rationale: /etc/gshadow holds group password hashes and administrator lists; it must not be readable or writable by non-root users.
checks.remediation: chown root:shadow /etc/gshadow && chmod 640 /etc/gshadow

checks.title: No world-writable files exist in key directories
checks.rationale: A world-writable file can be modified by any local user, which is a common path to privilege escalation or persistence if that file is ever executed or trusted by a privileged process.
checks.evidence: No world-writable regular files found under /tmp, /var/tmp, /home, /etc (20001 entries scanned (scan truncated at entry cap, more may exist)).
checks.remediation: For each reported file: chmod o-w <file>  (review the file's purpose first - some world-writable files, e.g. under a sticky-bit /tmp, are intentional).

checks.title: No unowned files or directories exist in key directories
checks.rationale: A file owned by a UID/GID with no corresponding account (e.g. left behind after a user was deleted) may be inadvertently accessible or reused by a future account created with a reused UID.
checks.evidence: No unowned files/directories found under /tmp, /var/tmp, /home, /etc (20001 entries scanned (scan truncated at entry cap, more may exist)).
checks.remediation: For each reported path: chown root:root <path>, or assign it to its correct owner after investigating why it's unowned.

checks.title: Local interactive user home directories are not group- or other-writable
checks.rationale: A group- or other-writable home directory lets other local users tamper with that account's dotfiles (e.g. plant a malicious .bashrc) to escalate privilege the next time the owner logs in.
checks.evidence: Checked 1 interactive user home director(ies); none are group/other writable.
checks.remediation: For each reported home directory: chmod g-w,o-w <home-dir>

checks.title: Default user umask is 027 or more restrictive
checks.rationale: A permissive default umask (e.g. 022) means every file a user creates is world-readable by default, including ones that shouldn't be.
checks.evidence: No UMASK setting found in /etc/login.defs (login.defs default of 022 applies).
checks.remediation: Set 'UMASK 027' in /etc/login.defs, and add 'umask 027' to /etc/profile.d/local-umask.sh for shell sessions.

checks.title: auditd is installed and enabled
checks.rationale: auditd provides a tamper-evident record of security-relevant events (file access, syscalls, auth events) that's essential for incident response and compliance - without it, a breach investigation has far less to work with.
checks.evidence: auditd is not installed (no auditctl binary, no /usr/sbin/auditd).
checks.remediation: apt install auditd audispd-plugins && systemctl --now enable auditd

checks.title: A system logging service (rsyslog or systemd-journald) is active
checks.rationale: Without a running log service, security-relevant events (auth failures, sudo use, service crashes) aren't captured anywhere, which blinds both real-time alerting and after-the-fact investigation.
checks.remediation: apt install rsyslog && systemctl --now enable rsyslog  (or ensure systemd-journald is running: systemctl --now enable systemd-journald)

checks.title: Authentication log file is not world-readable or writable
checks.rationale: Auth logs record login attempts and sudo usage; if readable by any local user they leak information useful for reconnaissance (valid usernames, login timing), and if writable by non-root they could be tampered with to cover an intruder's tracks.
checks.remediation: chmod 640 /var/log/auth.log && chown syslog:adm /var/log/auth.log

checks.title: cron is restricted to authorized users (cron.allow present, cron.deny absent)
checks.rationale: Without an allow-list, every local user can schedule their own cron jobs by default, which is a common persistence/privilege-escalation vector once an account is compromised.
checks.evidence: /etc/cron.allow exists=False, /etc/cron.deny exists=False (expected cron.allow to exist and cron.deny to not exist)
checks.remediation: touch /etc/cron.allow && chmod 600 /etc/cron.allow && rm -f /etc/cron.deny   # list only trusted usernames, one per line, in cron.allow

checks.title: IP forwarding is disabled
checks.rationale: A host that isn't meant to be a router shouldn't forward packets between interfaces - leaving it enabled widens the blast radius if the host is compromised and could be abused to pivot traffic.
checks.remediation: sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=0 && echo 'net.ipv4.ip_forward=0' >> /etc/sysctl.d/60-cis-hardening.conf

checks.title: ICMP redirects are not accepted
checks.rationale: Accepting ICMP redirects lets another host on the local network silently alter this host's routing table, a classic MITM technique.
checks.remediation: sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0 && echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0' >> /etc/sysctl.d/60-cis-hardening.conf

checks.title: Sending ICMP redirects is disabled
checks.rationale: A host that isn't a router shouldn't send ICMP redirects either - doing so can leak internal topology information and isn't needed for a non-routing host.
checks.remediation: sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects=0 && echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects=0' >> /etc/sysctl.d/60-cis-hardening.conf

checks.title: Reverse path filtering is enabled
checks.rationale: Reverse path filtering drops packets whose source address couldn't have legitimately arrived on the interface they came in on, which mitigates IP spoofing used in many DoS and MITM attacks.
checks.remediation: sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1 && echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1' >> /etc/sysctl.d/60-cis-hardening.conf

checks.title: TCP SYN cookies are enabled
checks.rationale: SYN cookies let the kernel keep accepting legitimate connections under a SYN-flood DoS attack instead of exhausting its backlog queue.
checks.remediation: sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1 && echo 'net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1' >> /etc/sysctl.d/60-cis-hardening.conf

checks.title: A host-based firewall (ufw/nftables/iptables) is installed and active
checks.rationale: A host-based firewall is a baseline defense-in-depth control even behind network firewalls/security groups - without one, every listening service on the host is directly reachable from anything that can route to it.
checks.evidence: No firewall tool found on PATH (checked ufw, nft, iptables) - no host-based firewall is installed.
checks.remediation: Install and enable one firewall: 'apt install ufw && ufw default deny incoming && ufw enable' is the simplest option for a single host.

checks.title: Legacy plaintext-protocol services (telnet/rsh/rlogin/tftp/NIS) are not installed
checks.rationale: These services transmit credentials and data in cleartext and have long-available encrypted replacements (SSH/SFTP). Their presence is almost always leftover cruft, not an intentional choice.
checks.evidence: No legacy service binaries found on PATH (checked: telnet server (in.telnetd), rsh server (rshd), rlogin server (rlogind), TFTP server (tftpd), NIS server (ypserv)).
checks.remediation: apt purge telnetd rsh-server rlogin nis tftpd-hpa  # remove whichever are installed

checks.title: Automatic security updates are configured
checks.rationale: Unpatched known vulnerabilities are one of the most common initial-access vectors. Automatic security updates close that gap without relying on a human to remember to patch.
checks.remediation: apt install unattended-upgrades && dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades

checks.title: Address space layout randomization (ASLR) is enabled
checks.rationale: ASLR randomizes where a process's memory regions are placed, making memory-corruption exploits (buffer overflows, etc.) substantially harder to reliably exploit.
checks.remediation: sysctl -w kernel.randomize_va_space=2 && echo 'kernel.randomize_va_space=2' >> /etc/sysctl.d/60-cis-hardening.conf

checks.title: Core dumps are restricted for SUID programs
checks.rationale: A core dump of a SUID program can leak sensitive memory contents (e.g. credentials handled by that process) to any local user who can read the resulting core file.
checks.remediation: sysctl -w fs.suid_dumpable=0 && echo 'fs.suid_dumpable=0' >> /etc/sysctl.d/60-cis-hardening.conf

checks.title: No passwordless (NOPASSWD) sudo entries are configured
checks.rationale: A NOPASSWD sudo rule means anyone with access to that account (e.g. via a stolen SSH key or an unattended session) gets root with no second factor - it collapses 'compromise the account' and 'compromise root' into the same event.
checks.evidence: None of /etc/sudoers are readable without root (expected mode 440) - cannot verify.
checks.remediation: Edit the offending file with visudo -f <file> and remove the NOPASSWD tag, requiring a password (or configure MFA-backed sudo) for privileged commands.

checks.title: SSH root login is disabled (PermitRootLogin no)
checks.rationale: Allowing SSH login directly as root removes the audit trail of which named account escalated, and gives a brute-forced/leaked root password or key immediate full access.
checks.evidence: openssh-server is not installed and no sshd_config exists on this host (checked `sshd -T` and /etc/ssh/sshd_config) - SSH hardening does not apply.
checks.remediation: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set 'PermitRootLogin no' then systemctl reload sshd

checks.title: SSH PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
checks.rationale: If empty passwords are permitted, any account with a blank password field could log in over SSH with no credential at all.
checks.evidence: openssh-server is not installed and no sshd_config exists on this host (checked `sshd -T` and /etc/ssh/sshd_config) - SSH hardening does not apply.
checks.remediation: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set 'PermitEmptyPasswords no' then systemctl reload sshd

checks.title: SSH password authentication is disabled (key-based auth only)
checks.rationale: Password authentication over SSH is subject to brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks; disabling it in favor of key-based auth removes that entire attack surface.
checks.evidence: openssh-server is not installed and no sshd_config exists on this host (checked `sshd -T` and /etc/ssh/sshd_config) - SSH hardening does not apply.
checks.remediation: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set 'PasswordAuthentication no', ensure your SSH key is deployed and working first, then systemctl reload sshd

checks.title: SSH MaxAuthTries is 4 or less
checks.rationale: A high MaxAuthTries lets an attacker attempt many password/key guesses within a single connection, speeding up brute-force attacks.
checks.evidence: openssh-server is not installed and no sshd_config exists on this host (checked `sshd -T` and /etc/ssh/sshd_config) - SSH hardening does not apply.
checks.remediation: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set 'MaxAuthTries 4' then systemctl reload sshd

checks.title: SSH X11Forwarding is disabled
checks.rationale: X11 forwarding over SSH is rarely needed on a server and expands attack surface (X11 has a long history of privilege-escalation and information-disclosure issues).
checks.evidence: openssh-server is not installed and no sshd_config exists on this host (checked `sshd -T` and /etc/ssh/sshd_config) - SSH hardening does not apply.
checks.remediation: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set 'X11Forwarding no' then systemctl reload sshd

checks.title: SSH warning banner is configured
checks.rationale: A pre-authentication banner (e.g. an authorized-use warning) is often a legal prerequisite for prosecuting unauthorized access and signals that the system is monitored.
checks.evidence: openssh-server is not installed and no sshd_config exists on this host (checked `sshd -T` and /etc/ssh/sshd_config) - SSH hardening does not apply.
checks.remediation: Create /etc/issue.net with a warning banner, then in /etc/ssh/sshd_config set 'Banner /etc/issue.net' and systemctl reload sshd
